﻿* Heat Pump
A heat pump doesn't generate heat by burning fuel or resistance heating — it moves existing low-grade heat (from ambient air, waste water, exhaust, or waste heat streams) up to a higher, usable temperature using a compressor cycle driven by electricity. Because it's moving heat rather than creating it from scratch, it can deliver more thermal energy out than electrical energy in — this is the key thing that makes it fundamentally different from an electric boiler. 




Field
	Value
	Process
	Hot water, low-pressure steam, drying, pasteurization — best suited to food processing, dairy, and low/medium-temperature textile processes
	Temperature
	Delivery side typically 60–200°C (mainstream commercial units cap around 150–160°C; specialized high-temperature heat pumps push toward 200°C+)
	Energy source
	Grid electricity + a low-grade heat source (ambient air, waste heat, effluent/wastewater)
	Efficiency (COP)
	Typically 2.5–5.0 (delivers 250–500% of the electrical energy input as heat), dropping at higher temperature lifts
	CAPEX
	



Industrial Heat Pump — CAPEX in ₹
Basis
	USD (original)
	₹ (converted )
	Per kWth (high-temp units)
	$1,500 – $4,000 / kWth
	₹1.43 lakh – ₹3.8 lakh per kWth
	Large-scale (per MW installed)
	$1 million – $3 million / MW
	₹9.5 crore – ₹28.5 crore per MW
	   
	OPEX
	Lower than electric boiler or fossil fuel per unit of heat delivered — but adds compressor maintenance
	Lifetime
	Generally 15–20 years for the compressor/mechanical system
	Space
	Compact core unit, but often needs space for heat exchangers, potential thermal storage, and access to a heat source (waste heat stream, cooling tower, etc.)
	Constraints
	Temperature ceiling, needs an accessible low-grade heat source, higher upfront cost, grid capacity
	



* Industrial Heat pump
An industrial heat pump (IHP) transfers heat from a low-temperature source such as waste heat, ambient air, water, wastewater, or industrial exhaust to a higher-temperature process. It does not generate heat by combustion; instead, it uses electricity to drive a refrigeration/heat-pump cycle. The system can recover otherwise wasted heat and upgrade it to a useful temperature for processes such as drying, washing, evaporation, pasteurization, and hot-water or steam generation.
Field
	Value
	Process
	Industrial hot-water generation, drying, washing, pasteurization, food processing, evaporation, distillation, space/process heating, and low- to medium-temperature steam generation. Particularly suitable where a continuous heat source or waste-heat stream is available.
	Temperature
	Conventional industrial heat pumps commonly supply heat up to ~80–120°C; advanced high-temperature heat pumps can reach approximately 150–200°C or higher, depending on technology, refrigerant, heat source and application.
	Energy source
	Primarily electricity to operate the compressor. The useful heat comes partly from the electricity and partly from the low-temperature heat source being upgraded.
	Efficiency
	Expressed as COP (Coefficient of Performance) rather than boiler efficiency. Typical industrial systems may have a COP of roughly 2–5, depending strongly on source temperature, required output temperature and temperature lift. Higher COP means less electricity per unit of useful heat.
	CAPEX
	Generally higher than a conventional fossil-fuel boiler for the same heat capacity, particularly for high-temperature systems. Cost varies significantly with capacity, temperature lift, heat exchangers, compressor technology, heat-source infrastructure and installation.
	OPEX
	Mainly electricity cost, plus maintenance and pumping/fan costs. OPEX can be very attractive when electricity is reasonably priced and the heat pump can recover inexpensive or waste heat.
	Lifetime
	Typically around 15–25 years for a properly maintained industrial system, although compressors, pumps, valves and controls may require servicing or replacement during the system's life.
	Space
	Relatively compact compared with biomass/coal systems, because there is no combustion chamber, fuel yard, chimney or ash-handling system. However, additional space may be required for heat exchangers, pumps, storage tanks and the heat-source system.
	Constraints
	Required output temperature, temperature lift, availability and temperature of the heat source, electricity price, compressor limitations, refrigerant selection, water quality, seasonal source-temperature variation and grid capacity.
	Existing equipment replaced
	Can replace or reduce the operation of gas, oil, coal or electric boilers for suitable low/medium-temperature processes. It can also be installed as a pre-heating system before an existing boiler, reducing fossil-fuel consumption.
	Emissions
	No direct combustion emissions at the installation because there is no fuel combustion. Indirect CO₂ emissions depend on the electricity source. Using renewable electricity can significantly reduce lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions.
	Main advantage
	Very high energy efficiency because it moves heat rather than directly generating it. It can also recover waste heat that would otherwise be rejected to the environment.
	Main disadvantage
	Performance decreases as the required temperature difference (temperature lift) increases. High-temperature applications can have higher CAPEX and lower COP.
	Best suited for
	Industries with low/medium-temperature heat demand and an available waste-heat source, such as food & beverage, dairy, textiles, chemicals, paper, wastewater treatment and drying applications.
	Key calculation — COP
The most important parameter for comparing an industrial heat pump is:
COP= Q useful / W electricity
Where:
* Q useful​ = useful heat delivered
* W electricity​ = electrical energy consumed by compressor and auxiliaries.

* Electric resistance heating
Electric resistance heating uses electricity to produce heat through a resistance heating element. When electric current passes through the element, electrical energy is converted directly into heat. It does not require combustion, fuel storage, or a chimney, making it a simple and compact option for industrial process heating.
Field
	Value
	Process
	Direct process heating, air heating, drying, ovens, furnaces, curing, water heating, pre-heating and other industrial heating applications
	Temperature
	Typically up to ~400°C for common industrial resistance-heating applications; specialized heaters can reach higher temperatures
	Energy source
	Grid electricity; 3-phase electricity is generally required for larger industrial systems
	Efficiency
	Typically ~95–100% at the point of use, because almost all electrical energy is converted into heat
	CAPEX
	Approximately ₹1–5 lakh for small systems and ₹5–25 lakh+ for medium industrial systems, depending on power rating, heater type, temperature and installation
	OPEX
	Mainly electricity cost; maintenance is relatively low, but operating cost depends strongly on electricity tariff
	Lifetime
	Typically 10–20 years for the overall system; heating elements may need replacement earlier depending on temperature and operating hours
	Space
	Very compact — no chimney, fuel storage or large boiler house is required
	Constraints
	Electricity tariff, available grid capacity, 3-phase power for larger systems, grid reliability, high power demand and heating-element replacement
	* Additional important points
Field
	Value
	Existing equipment it can replace/reduce
	Gas, diesel, coal, LPG or furnace-oil direct-heating systems; can also replace some hot-air and fuel-fired heating equipment
	Maintenance required
	Heating-element inspection/replacement, electrical connection checking, temperature-controller maintenance and cleaning
	Backup required?
	Usually not mandatory, but backup power or another heater may be needed where continuous production is critical
	Thermal storage
	Generally not required because heat can be produced directly when electricity is available
	Emissions reduction
	Can reduce direct CO₂ and combustion emissions because there is no on-site fuel combustion; total emissions depend on the electricity source/grid mix
	Best suited for
	Textile, food processing, drying, ovens, bakeries, plastics, chemical processing, metal processing and other MSMEs requiring direct low/medium-temperature heat
	*  MSME optimizer
* Electricity → Resistance element → Heat → Industrial process
* It is most attractive when the MSME has sufficient electrical capacity and competitive electricity tariffs, especially where precise and direct heating is required.
